# Zentinel: site writing in full

> A security-first reverse proxy built on Pingora: explicit configuration, bounded resources, and WAF and auth in isolated agents.

## What Zentinel is

Zentinel is a security-first reverse proxy built to guard the free web. It is written in Rust on Cloudflare's [Pingora](https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora), through a fork published on crates.io as `zentinel-pingora-*`.

- **Configuration:** KDL, in one file or several joined with `include`. Validated with `zentinel test`; `zentinel lint` reports settings that are being ignored. Reloaded on `SIGHUP`, or on file change with `auto-reload`, and validated before an atomic swap.
- **Routing and upstreams:** routes match on host and path; load balancing includes round robin, least connections, consistent hashing, Maglev and power of two choices; active health checks over HTTP, TCP and gRPC; retries and circuit breakers.
- **TLS:** termination with per-SNI certificates, client certificates (mTLS) and ACME issuance. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 downstream and upstream; HTTP/3 is not implemented.
- **Traffic handling:** response caching, rate limiting, GeoIP filtering (MaxMind and IP2Location databases), response compression with gzip, Brotli or zstd negotiated from `Accept-Encoding`, and static file serving.
- **Agents:** WAF, authentication and other policy run in agents, separate processes the proxy talks to over Unix domain sockets or gRPC (optionally with TLS) using agent protocol v2. Each agent has its own timeout and a `failure-mode` of open or closed, so a slow or crashed agent does not take the proxy down. The [agent registry](https://registry.zentinelproxy.io/) lists agents for WAF and ModSecurity rules, bot management, IP reputation, authentication and SPIFFE identity, GraphQL, gRPC and SOAP inspection, and scripting in Lua, JavaScript or WebAssembly. SDKs for writing agents exist for Rust, Go, Python, TypeScript, Kotlin, Elixir and Haskell.
- **Observability:** Prometheus metrics and structured access, error and audit logs. OpenTelemetry tracing and Redis or memcached-backed distributed rate limiting are build features (`opentelemetry`, `distributed-rate-limit`), not in the default build.
- **Licence:** Apache 2.0.

The index of every page is at https://zentinelproxy.io/llms.txt; the documentation is at https://docs.zentinelproxy.io/.

================================================================================

# Compare

URL: https://zentinelproxy.io/compare/
Updated: 2026-10-18

> How Zentinel differs from nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Caddy and Traefik — on design, not on benchmarks.

Zentinel is a reverse proxy built on Cloudflare's [Pingora](https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora) in Rust. The proxies below are mature, widely deployed, and each is the right choice for many workloads. This page compares **design choices**, not speed: we make no performance claims here, and the [benchmarks page](https://zentinelproxy.io/benchmarks/) explains how our own measurements were made and where they fall short.

Facts about other projects are kept to their well-known, documented behaviour as of October 2026. If something here is wrong or out of date, please [open an issue](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinelproxy.io/issues).

## At a glance

### Language and configuration

<div style="overflow-x: auto">

| | Language | Configuration | Reload |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Zentinel** | Rust | KDL file(s) | `SIGHUP`, or file watch with `auto-reload`; config validated before an atomic swap |
| **nginx** | C | `nginx.conf` | Graceful reload (`nginx -s reload`) |
| **HAProxy** | C | `haproxy.cfg` | Seamless reload (master-worker), runtime API |
| **Envoy** | C++ | YAML/JSON, or xDS APIs | Dynamic via xDS; hot restart |
| **Caddy** | Go | Caddyfile or JSON (admin API) | Graceful reload via admin API |
| **Traefik** | Go | Static file plus dynamic providers (files, Docker labels, Kubernetes CRDs) | Automatic from providers |

</div>

### Extensions and WAF

<div style="overflow-x: auto">

| | Extension model | WAF |
|---|---|---|
| **Zentinel** | External agents (separate processes over Unix sockets or gRPC); WebAssembly modules through the WASM agent | As agents: native Rust WAF, pure-Rust ModSecurity/CRS engine, or libmodsecurity |
| **nginx** | C modules, njs; Lua via OpenResty | Third-party ModSecurity connector; commercial F5 products |
| **HAProxy** | Lua; SPOE (external agents) | Commercial (HAProxy Enterprise), or via SPOE |
| **Envoy** | C++ filters, Lua, Wasm (proxy-wasm); `ext_authz`/`ext_proc` external services | Via Wasm or external filters (e.g. Coraza) |
| **Caddy** | Go modules compiled in (`xcaddy`) | Third-party modules (e.g. Coraza) |
| **Traefik** | Go plugins (Yaegi) and Wasm plugins | Plugins; commercial offerings |

</div>

### TLS and protocols

<div style="overflow-x: auto">

| | ACME (automatic certificates) | HTTP/3 (QUIC) |
|---|---|---|
| **Zentinel** | Built in: HTTP-01, DNS-01 (Cloudflare, Hetzner, webhook), EAB, ARI | **Not implemented** (an `h3` listener is rejected at startup) |
| **nginx** | External client traditionally; official ACME module since 2025 | Yes |
| **HAProxy** | External client traditionally; native ACME added in 3.2 | Yes |
| **Envoy** | Not built in (typically cert-manager / SDS) | Yes |
| **Caddy** | Built in, on by default | Yes, on by default |
| **Traefik** | Built in | Yes |

</div>

### Kubernetes, observability and license

<div style="overflow-x: auto">

| | Kubernetes Gateway API | Observability | License |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Zentinel** | `zentinel-gateway` controller (targets Gateway API v1.4.1; conformance work in progress) | Prometheus metrics, access logs; OpenTelemetry tracing behind the `opentelemetry` build feature | Apache-2.0 |
| **nginx** | Separate project (NGINX Gateway Fabric) | Logs, `stub_status`; exporters and OTel module | BSD-2-Clause |
| **HAProxy** | Separate controller projects | Built-in Prometheus exporter, stats, logs | GPL-2.0 |
| **Envoy** | Separate projects (e.g. Envoy Gateway) | Extensive stats, admin endpoint, tracing | Apache-2.0 |
| **Caddy** | No official controller | Prometheus metrics, logs | Apache-2.0 |
| **Traefik** | Built-in provider | Prometheus, OpenTelemetry | MIT |

</div>

## Where Zentinel is different

**Complexity lives outside the core.** Anything parsing-heavy or policy-rich — WAF inspection, authentication, custom business logic — runs in an [agent](https://docs.zentinelproxy.io/agents/), a separate process the proxy talks to over a Unix socket or gRPC, with its own timeout and an explicit `failure-mode` of `open` or `closed`. An agent can crash, restart or be upgraded without taking the proxy down. HAProxy's SPOE and Envoy's `ext_authz`/`ext_proc` follow a similar out-of-process idea; in Zentinel it is the primary extension model rather than one option among in-process alternatives. Agent SDKs exist for Rust, Go, Python, TypeScript, Elixir, Kotlin and Haskell.

**Explicit configuration, checked before it runs.** Limits and timeouts are written in the config rather than implied. `zentinel lint` reports settings that parse but are read by nothing, and a reload that fails validation leaves the running configuration in place. See the [manifesto](https://zentinelproxy.io/manifesto/) for why.

**No vendor lock-in by design.** Zentinel is a single open-source project; WAF engines, ACME and the Gateway API controller are not reserved for a commercial edition. Releases are [signed and ship with SBOMs](https://zentinelproxy.io/supply-chain/).

## Where another proxy is the better choice

- **You need HTTP/3 today.** Zentinel does not implement QUIC yet.
- **You are building a service mesh** or already run an xDS control plane: Envoy and the meshes built on it are designed for that.
- **You want the widest ecosystem, documentation and operational experience**: nginx and HAProxy have decades of production history and extensive module ecosystems.
- **You want zero-configuration HTTPS for a small site**: Caddy enables ACME and HTTP/3 by default with very little configuration.
- **Your routing is driven by Docker labels or Kubernetes annotations**: Traefik's provider model is built around exactly that.

## In more depth

The documentation has a longer, side-by-side comparison with configuration examples: [Comparison with alternatives](https://docs.zentinelproxy.io/concepts/comparison/). The [features page](https://zentinelproxy.io/features/) lists what Zentinel does, and the [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) records what changed and when.

================================================================================

# Contributing

URL: https://zentinelproxy.io/contributing/
Updated: 2026-10-18

> How to contribute to Zentinel: where to start, what belongs in the core, and where to ask questions.

Zentinel sits at the edge of the web, so changes affect availability, security and someone's on-call. The bar is intentionally high, but small contributions are genuinely welcome: a clearer error message is a real improvement.

## Start here

- **Read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)** in the main repository. It explains what belongs in the core, what should be an agent instead, and what a change needs (limits, observability, tests, docs).
- **Read the [manifesto](https://zentinelproxy.io/manifesto/).** Proposals are judged against it: bounded, observable, explicit.
- **Pick an issue.** Issues labelled [`good-first-issue`](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/labels/good-first-issue) are scoped tasks that do not need deep knowledge of the proxy internals; [`help-wanted`](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/labels/help-wanted) marks issues where outside help is particularly welcome.

Good places to begin, even without a labelled issue: crate documentation, configuration error messages, tests for edge cases in `zentinel-config`, and KDL examples in `config/examples/`.

## Build an agent instead

Policy engines, scripting runtimes and business-specific logic do not belong in the core proxy; they belong in **agents**, external processes the proxy calls over a bounded protocol. If your idea is one of those, an agent is usually the faster path, and it can live in its own repository on its own release schedule.

SDKs are available for:

- [Rust](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel-agent-rust-sdk)
- [Go](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel-agent-go-sdk)
- [Python](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel-agent-python-sdk)
- [TypeScript](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel-agent-typescript-sdk)
- [Elixir](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel-agent-elixir-sdk)
- [Kotlin](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel-agent-kotlin-sdk)
- [Haskell](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel-agent-haskell-sdk)

The protocol is documented in the [agent docs](https://docs.zentinelproxy.io/agents/), and published agents are listed in the [agent registry](https://registry.zentinelproxy.io).

## Ask questions

- **[GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/discussions)** for questions, ideas and design discussion before you write code.
- **[GitHub Issues](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues)** for bugs and concrete feature requests.
- **Security issues** go through the private process on the [security page](https://zentinelproxy.io/security/), never a public issue.

## Other repositories

The website (this site) lives in [zentinelproxy/zentinelproxy.io](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinelproxy.io) and the documentation in [zentinelproxy/zentinelproxy.io-docs](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinelproxy.io-docs). Corrections to either are welcome as pull requests.

Please follow the [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

================================================================================

# Security

URL: https://zentinelproxy.io/security/
Updated: 2026-10-18

> How to report a vulnerability in Zentinel, which versions receive fixes, and how to verify what you deploy.

Zentinel sits at the edge of the network, so we treat security reports as the highest-priority work we have. This page summarises the project's [security policy](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/blob/main/SECURITY.md); where the two differ, `SECURITY.md` in the repository is authoritative.

## Reporting a vulnerability

**Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues.**

Report them privately via GitHub:

- **[GitHub private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/security/advisories/new)** on the `zentinelproxy/zentinel` repository, or
- contact **[@raffaelschneider](https://github.com/raffaelschneider)** directly via GitHub.

Please include:

1. **Description** — what is the vulnerability?
2. **Impact** — what can an attacker do with it?
3. **Reproduction** — steps to reproduce the issue
4. **Affected versions** — which versions are affected?
5. **Suggested fix** — if you have one

### What to expect

- **Acknowledgment** within 48 hours
- **Initial assessment** within 7 days
- **Resolution**, depending on severity: critical 24–48 hours, high 7 days, medium 30 days, low in the next release

We follow coordinated disclosure, credit reporters unless you prefer to remain anonymous, and publish a security advisory once a fix is available.

A machine-readable contact file is published at [`/.well-known/security.txt`](https://zentinelproxy.io/.well-known/security.txt) ([RFC 9116](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116)).

## Supported versions

Security fixes are shipped as a new release on the latest line. **Only the latest release is supported**; there are no long-term-support branches. Releases use [CalVer](https://docs.zentinelproxy.io/appendix/versioning/) (`YY.MM_PATCH`), and the corresponding crates are published on the 0.6.x line on crates.io. The [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) maps each release to its crate version and lists the advisories it addresses.

If you run an older release, upgrade to the latest one; the [upgrade guide](https://docs.zentinelproxy.io/operations/upgrade-guide/) describes the procedure.

## Verifying releases

Every release binary is signed with Sigstore cosign (keyless, tied to the project's GitHub Actions identity), container images on GHCR are signed and carry an SBOM attestation, and each release ships SBOMs in CycloneDX and SPDX formats along with SLSA provenance. The [supply chain security](https://zentinelproxy.io/supply-chain/) page has the exact verification commands.

## Advisories and security updates

Published advisories are listed on the repository's [GitHub Security Advisories](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/security/advisories) page. Security-relevant dependency updates, including RUSTSEC and GHSA identifiers, are recorded in the *Security* section of each [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) entry and announced with each [GitHub release](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/releases).

## Security design

Zentinel's approach follows the [manifesto](https://zentinelproxy.io/manifesto/): explicit limits and timeouts instead of hidden defaults, bounded resources, security logic isolated in external agents rather than the core, and every decision observable in logs and metrics. Two points about agents are worth stating plainly:

- The proxy runs every agent **out of process**, over a Unix domain socket or gRPC, so a fault in an agent, including a Wasmtime vulnerability in the WASM agent, stays in that agent's process. The zentinel repository also contains an in-process WebAssembly runtime (`zentinel-wasm-runtime`, moved to wasmtime 49 in 26.10_3), but the proxy binary does not use it.
- Agent traffic over Unix domain sockets is not encrypted; use gRPC with TLS for agents in sensitive environments.

================================================================================

# Why Zentinel Runs on a Fork of Pingora

URL: https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/why-we-fork-pingora/
Published: 2026-10-20

> Twice this year we wrote that our Pingora fork was temporary, kept only until upstream caught up on a security fix. It is still here, it is now published on crates.io, and it no longer exists for security reasons. Here is what it changes, why a proxy needs those changes, and what keeping a fork actually costs.

Zentinel is built on [Pingora](https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora),
Cloudflare's Rust framework for building proxies. For most of this year we have
also run on a fork of it, and we have said more than once that the fork was
about to go away.

In February, the [Pingora 0.7 post](https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/pingora-0-7-upgrade/) was titled
"Dropping the Fork". In March, the [0.8 post](https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/pingora-0-8-upgrade/)
said the fork was back, but only until 0.8.1 or 0.9.0 shipped. The
[CVE response post](https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/pingora-cve-response/) put it as a rule: we
maintain a fork only when upstream is behind on a security patch.

Pingora 0.9.0 shipped in September. The fork did not go away. Since August it
has carried changes that are not security fixes at all, and since August it has
been published on crates.io under its own names. This post explains why, and
what it costs us.

## The short version

Our fork today is upstream Pingora 0.9.0 plus three changes:

| Change | What it lets Zentinel do |
|---|---|
| `TlsSettings::with_server_config` | Hand the listener a complete rustls `ServerConfig`: the TLS versions, cipher suites and session settings from the configuration |
| `ProxyHttp::should_retry_response` | Retry a request when the upstream *answers* with an error such as `503`, not only when the connection fails |
| `Session::enable_retry_buffering_with_limit` | Keep request bodies larger than 64 KiB available for the upstream after the proxy has read them |

All three are additive. Each one defaults to upstream's behaviour, and none of
them changes anything for a program that does not call it. Five of Pingora's
crates are republished as `zentinel-pingora-*`, because they contain the
changes or depend on a crate that does. The rest are unchanged, and Zentinel
takes them straight from crates.io.

## How a security fork became a feature fork

The first two forks were what we said they were. In January we carried three
security fixes on Pingora 0.6 until 0.7 included them. In March we carried one
commit on 0.8.0 to move a transitive `prometheus` dependency past a
vulnerability. Both times the plan was to delete the fork, and the first time we
did.

What changed in August was not Pingora. It was what we were finding in
Zentinel. We spent August to October hunting for settings that parse,
validate and then do nothing, which we wrote about in
[It Parsed, and Did Nothing](https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/it-parsed-and-did-nothing/). Two of the
worst ones could not be fixed inside Zentinel at all.

**TLS settings with nowhere to go.** A Zentinel listener accepts per-SNI
certificates, client certificate authentication (`client-auth`), a minimum
TLS version and a cipher suite list. All of it was parsed and validated, and
none of it reached the listener ([#303](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues/303)).

The reason was in Pingora: `TlsSettings::build()` constructed its rustls
`ServerConfig` internally, with one certificate for every client, TLS 1.2 and
1.3, and the provider's default cipher suites. The `ServerConfig` never left
that function, so there was no way to give it anything else. Zentinel was
reduced to logging warnings that the configured certificates were not served
and the configured `client-auth` was not enforced.

The patch ([fork #6](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/pingora/pull/6)) adds
`TlsSettings::with_server_config`, which takes a `ServerConfig` the caller has
built. Zentinel builds one from the listener's configuration, with an SNI
certificate resolver, a client certificate verifier and the configured versions
and suites. `enable_h2()` still layers ALPN on top, so HTTP/2 keeps working. If
a client certificate verifier was also set the old way, it is reported rather
than dropped quietly: for mTLS in particular, silence would suggest an
enforcement that is not there.

**Retries that could not see a response.** A route's `retry-policy` is meant
to say things like "retry on `502` or `503`, three times"
([#279](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues/279)). Pingora's retry
loop runs again only when proxying returns an *error*. An upstream answering
`503` is not an error; it is a response, and by the time its status is known it
is already on its way to the client.

The patch ([fork #8](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/pingora/pull/8)) adds
`should_retry_response`, which sees the upstream's response header before any
of it is sent downstream. Returning `true` turns the response into a retryable
error, and Pingora's existing retry loop does the rest, including replaying the
buffered request body. It never fires for cached responses, for `1xx`, or when
the body was too large to buffer, because a retry would send a truncated body.
Counting attempts is left to the application, which is what makes per-route
limits possible: Pingora's `max_retries` is one number for the whole server.

The third change came this month. Zentinel reads a request's whole body before
proxying it when it validates the body against an API schema or multiplexes MCP
calls. The body then reaches the upstream through Pingora's retry buffer, which
has a fixed size of 64 KiB. Anything larger was dropped from the buffer, the
upstream waited for a body that never came, and the request timed out
([#531](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues/531)). The patch
([fork #12](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/pingora/pull/12)) lets the caller
choose the buffer size per request.

## Pingora is a framework, and frameworks have edges

None of this is a complaint about Pingora. It is a framework with deliberate
extension points, `ProxyHttp`'s filters and callbacks, and almost everything
Zentinel does fits through them. Routing, agents, caching, rate limiting, health
checks and the WAF all live on our side of that line.

But a general-purpose reverse proxy driven by a configuration file has a
specific problem. Every setting it accepts must reach something that can apply
it. A framework is shaped by the programs its authors write against it. A
configuration language is shaped by what operators expect to be able to say.
Where those two shapes differ, the proxy either refuses the setting, which
operators rightly find limiting, or accepts it and ignores it. That is the bug
class we spent three months removing.

So when a setting ran into one of Pingora's edges, we had three options. Drop
the setting. Keep it and document that it does nothing. Or move the edge. For
TLS settings and response-based retries, moving the edge was a few dozen lines
in Pingora against a feature that otherwise could not work, so we moved it.

Upstream is moving too. Pingora 0.9.0 added `set_cert_resolver` and
`set_client_cert_verifier`, which close part of the TLS gap: per-SNI
certificates and mTLS could now be done without our patch. Protocol versions,
cipher suites and session settings still cannot, so the patch stays for now.

We have not proposed these changes upstream. They are written to be additive
and off by default, so they could be.

## What a fork costs

We said in February that a fork is operational overhead. Here is the bill so
far.

**Publishing.** `cargo publish` keeps only the version of a dependency and
drops its git source. Zentinel depended on the fork by git URL, so the
`zentinel-proxy` crate on crates.io depended on *upstream* Pingora, which lacks
`with_server_config`. `cargo install zentinel-proxy` built for ten minutes and
then failed to compile, for two releases, until a user reported it
([#357](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues/357)). Our release
binaries and container images were fine, which is why we did not notice.

The fix was to publish the fork's crates under new names
([fork #9](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/pingora/pull/9)), and that had a
trap of its own. Every crate above `pingora-core` in the dependency graph has to
be renamed too, or a build ends up with two incompatible copies of Pingora's
types. Our first attempt built cleanly on its own and failed the moment Zentinel
was built against it, because the fork resolved one crate from a local path and
Zentinel resolved it from crates.io. A fork that builds green by itself tells
you nothing about how it behaves once published.

**Rebasing.** Moving the fork to 0.9.0
([fork #10](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/pingora/pull/10)) was mostly
mechanical: take upstream's version of every file outside the patch set, then
merge the patch set by hand. The one surprise was a test file the fork had never
touched. Git merged it from an older common ancestor and silently put back test
gating that upstream had removed in 0.9.0. We now finish every rebase by diffing
the result against the upstream tag and resetting anything outside the patch
set.

**Keeping the fork's own CI alive.** A fork inherits upstream's CI and then
drifts from it. Our fork's build went red for months because upstream does not
commit a `Cargo.lock`, and new releases of its dependencies broke the build on
their own schedule. Its security audit failed on every run for more than 60
days, because the action it used stopped resolving. Neither failure was in code we had
changed, and both were easy to miss, because nobody watches a repository they
think of as "upstream plus two patches".

**Attribution.** Pingora is Apache-2.0. The fork carries a `NOTICE` that names
the modified files and what changed, and says that Zentinel is not affiliated
with or endorsed by Cloudflare. The renamed crates on crates.io point at our
fork, not at Cloudflare's repository, so that nobody files an issue with
Cloudflare about code Cloudflare did not write.

## Where this goes next

The fork has a clear exit for each patch. When upstream can take a full rustls
configuration, `with_server_config` goes. If upstream gains a way to retry on a
response, `should_retry_response` goes. When the retry buffer size can be set
per request, the third goes.

Upstream is already heading somewhere we want to follow. A change merged after
0.9.0 makes Pingora's response body filters `async`. Today those filters are
synchronous, so when a Zentinel agent inspects a response body, the proxy has
to block a worker thread while it waits for the agent. When we fixed the other
blocking calls on the request path in
[26.10_7](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md),
this was the one we could not remove. Once that change is released, it goes
away without a patch of ours.

Until then, the honest description is the one we should have written in
August: Zentinel runs on a small, published fork of Pingora, because a proxy
that promises to apply its configuration sometimes needs a hook the framework
does not have yet. The fork, its pull requests and the reasoning behind each
patch are public at
[zentinelproxy/pingora](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/pingora).

================================================================================

# It Parsed, and Did Nothing

URL: https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/it-parsed-and-did-nothing/
Published: 2026-10-19

> Between August and October we fixed more than a dozen Zentinel features that were accepted, validated and logged as running, and had no effect. Timeouts, failure modes, TLS settings, health checks, agents, WAF rules. None of them produced an error, because none of them failed. Here is the shape they share, why ordinary testing cannot see it, and the checks that catch it now.

Most bugs announce themselves. A request fails, a log line turns red, a test
breaks. This post is about the other kind, the kind we spent most of August,
September and October finding in Zentinel: a setting that parses, validates,
shows up in the startup log, and does nothing at all.

We found more than a dozen of them. They were in timeouts, route policies, TLS,
retries, health checks, agents, caching and the WAF engine. Most were in
configurations we ship ourselves. Every one had been accepted by every check we
had. This is an account of what they had in common, and of what we changed so
that the next one is caught by a machine instead of by luck.

The release-by-release detail is in the
[26.09–26.10 roundup](https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/zentinel-26-09-26-10/) and the
[CHANGELOG](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
This post is about the pattern.

## The inventory

A selection, all fixed and released:

| What the config said | What actually happened | Fixed in |
|---|---|---|
| `request-secs 300` on an upstream | The parser read `request`, so the 60s default applied | 26.08_4 |
| `failure-mode "open"` on a route | Never read; every route ran fail-closed | 26.08_4 |
| WAF rule `exclusions { … }` | Looked for one level too high; every exclusion dropped | 26.08_4 |
| `retry-policy { max-attempts 3 }` | Retried *backend selection*, not the request | 26.08_4 |
| Per-SNI certs, `client-auth`, `min-version` | Parsed, validated, then never reached the listener | 26.08_3 |
| An `mcp { tools { allow … } }` policy | Evaluator correct, never called from the request path | 26.08_5 |
| `tracing { enabled #false }` | Read by nothing; tracing stayed on | 26.08_10 |
| Upstream `discovery` blocks | Parsed into nothing; the upstream routed nowhere | 26.08_11 |
| `health-check { … }`, every type | The checker probed an empty backend set | 26.09_2 |
| An agent behind `failure-mode "open"` | Unreachable in the container images; traffic passed uninspected | 26.09_3, 26.09_4 |

Two things stand out. The first is that, in the configuration cases, the
**documentation was right**. `failure-mode "open"` was documented; the code
ignored it. Every one of these fixes moved the code toward the docs, never the
other way. Nothing was checking the two against each other.

The second is the direction of failure. Not one of them failed toward an error.
They all failed toward "your intent was discarded and a default was applied",
and the defaults were plausible enough that nobody noticed.

## Silent in both directions

The health-check bug is the cleanest example, and we have written about it
[before](https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/the-gateway-for-agentic-protocols/#what-we-found-while-building-it),
so briefly. Until 26.09_2, this block was inert:

```kdl
health-check {
    type "http" {
        path "/healthz"
        expected-status 200
    }
    interval-secs 2
    timeout-secs 1
    unhealthy-threshold 2
    healthy-threshold 2
}
```

The runner started. It logged `Starting health check runner`. It ticked every
two seconds. It sent nothing, because the set of backends it iterated was never
populated. Measured against a real fixture: **0 probes in twelve seconds before
the fix, 29 after.**

"Silent in both directions" is the important part. A missing probe cannot fail,
so no error is ever raised. And no backend is ever marked unhealthy, so nothing
visible ever changes: traffic keeps flowing to every backend, which is exactly
what a healthy fleet looks like. The only way to tell "health checking works and
all backends are healthy" from "health checking does nothing" is to look at the
backend and count.

Agents had the same property, from a different angle. With
`failure-mode "open"`, an agent the proxy cannot reach means requests are
forwarded unprocessed. That is the documented, intended behaviour. It is also
indistinguishable, from the outside, from a working agent that found nothing
worth blocking.

## Why none of it showed up

We had tests. We had `zentinel validate`. We had startup logging. Each of them
was answering a slightly different question from the one that mattered.

**Defaults that look right.** The shipped config wrote
`idle-timeout-secs 60` while the parser read `idle-timeout`. The default is 60,
so reading the setting back gave the right answer while discarding it entirely.
The same happened with `memcached-ttl-secs 2` (default 2) and
`redis-fallback-local #true` (default true). The setting that mattered was
`redis-fallback-local #false`: an operator turning off local fallback, so that a
Redis outage does not quietly split one global rate limit into one limit per
proxy, got local fallback anyway.

**"It started" is not "it works".** A log line saying a subsystem started is
evidence that a constructor ran. The health checker, the agent pool and the
discovery code all started, logged and reported success.

**Tests that construct the thing under test.** The TLS SNI tests, 28 of them,
called the certificate resolver directly and passed. The bug was that the
listener never consulted the resolver, which no test that calls the resolver
can see. Our [MCP post](https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/header-says-read-body-says-delete/#the-correction)
carries a correction for the same reason: seventy-three policy tests built a
policy object by hand and evaluated it, and production never built one.

**Tests that could not fail.** One container test checked that the echo agent
had run by grepping the response for `Correlation`. That matches the proxy's own
`X-Correlation-Id`, so it passed with the agent stopped. A regression test for
the `Cache-Status` fix (26.08_12, where a Zentinel in front of another cache
erased that cache's entry from the header) was first written against the helper
that builds the header value, and passed with the bug put back.

**A warning nobody reads.** Route parsing already warned about unrecognised
children. A `circuit-breaker` block inside a route, which only upstreams and
agents support, appeared in our own default config, so the warning fired on
every startup for months. A log line is not a guardrail.

## The WAF engine had it too

[zentinel-modsec](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel-modsec), our
pure-Rust ModSecurity engine, has run into this shape more than once; the
[June post](https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/pure-rust-modsecurity-crs-v4/) was about the first round.
In August, the published 0.3.0 loaded stock OWASP CRS v4 without complaint and
then denied every request, including `GET /`.

Four defects, each hiding another
([#29](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel-modsec/issues/29)). The one
that blocked everything: `REQUEST_LINE` was not implemented, so it resolved to
nothing, and CRS rule 920100 tests it with a *negated* operator. "Nothing to
test", negated, became "matched", on every request. Underneath that,
`skipAfter` in phase 2 discarded the rest of the phase, so the anomaly-score
check that makes CRS's blocking decision could never run, and `TX` keys were
case-sensitive, so scores never accumulated.

What is instructive is why the upstream CRS regression corpus barely noticed.
It runs in `DetectionOnly` mode at paranoia level 4, which skips the blocking
decision entirely and keeps the paranoia gates from firing. It measures whether
individual rules *match*, not whether the WAF *decides*. Against the corpus,
the fix moved the pass rate from 81.1% to 81.5%. Run the same corpus in the
shape people deploy (blocking, paranoia 1) and it went from 19.9% to 54.4%.

All four are fixed in zentinel-modsec
[0.4.0](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel-modsec/releases/tag/v0.4.0),
released 31 August; 0.3.0 has been yanked from crates.io.
The ZentinelSec agent depends on 0.4.0 on its main branch; a tagged agent
release that includes it has not been cut yet.

## What changed

None of the fixes above is interesting on its own; most were a line or two.
What we changed is how we look.

### Probe behaviour; do not grep

Grep is actively misleading for this class of bug. When we went looking for why
route `rate-limit` did nothing, the string `rate_limit` appeared four times in
the config parser. That reads like it is handled. None of the four was an
assignment.

What works is to parse a config and read the result back: what did the struct
end up holding? For runtime behaviour, it means measuring at the other end:
count probes arriving at a fixture, assert a header that only the agent emits
arrives at the upstream, time a retry to see whether the backoff happened. The
retry work found an off-by-one where the first retry ran with no delay. Behaviour
looked fine; only the 57ms that should have been 150ms gave it away.

### Test against a non-default value

If the value you test with equals the default, the test cannot distinguish "the
setting works" from "the setting is ignored". This is the single rule that would
have caught the most of these, and it is easy to break by accident, because the
natural thing to test is the value in the example config.

### Make every test able to fail

Before trusting a regression test, put the bug back and run it. If it still
passes, it was never testing the fix. For agents: stop the agent and re-run. For
the WAF: zentinel-modsec now has CI for the first time, with a conformance job
that ratchets the CRS corpus pass count upward, and a separate test that asserts
the *blocking decision* in deployed shape, since the corpus alone cannot see
that. Both gates were shown to fail before they were trusted.

### Lint the configuration for keys nothing reads

KDL is permissive by design, and Zentinel's parsers read the keys they know and
skip the rest. That is how `request-sec` (one letter short) or `failure_mode`
(underscore) disappear without a trace. This config validates:

```kdl
upstream "inference" {
    target "10.0.0.1:8000"
    target "10.0.0.2:8000"
    timeouts {
        connect-secs 2
        request-sec 300
    }
}
```

```kdl
route "chat" {
    matches {
        path-prefix "/v1/chat"
    }
    upstream "inference"
    policies {
        failure_mode "open"
    }
}
```

and runs with a 60-second request timeout and a fail-closed route. Since
[#365](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues/365), `zentinel lint`
reports both:

```
'request-sec' is not a setting in the 'timeouts' block and is being ignored. Did you mean 'request-secs'?
'failure_mode' is not a setting in the 'policies' block and is being ignored. Did you mean 'failure-mode'?
```

It checks 43 blocks and catches three mechanisms. Unknown keys are the obvious
one. The second is a key written in the wrong one of two same-named blocks:
`backend "disk"` inside a route's `cache` block parses and does nothing, because
the storage backend is set in the top-level `cache` block, and the lint now says
so. The third surprised us. KDL treats everything up to a newline or `;` as one
node, so a block written on one line:

```kdl
listener "public" { address "0.0.0.0:8080" protocol "http" }
```

is a single `address` node with three arguments. The parser reads the first
argument and there is no `protocol` child to find. The lint reports it:

```
'protocol' is being read as an argument to 'address' rather than as a setting,
so it is ignored. In the 'listener' block, put each setting on its own line
(or separate them with ';').
```

Two design choices keep the lint honest. Each block's list of valid keys lives
next to its parser, not in a separate file, because two copies of a key list is
how this bug comes back. And a test runs the check over every config we ship and
fails the build if any of them uses a key nothing reads. On its first run, that
test found `verify #true` in an example config's upstream TLS block, where the
real key is `insecure-skip-verify`.

The [playground](https://zentinelproxy.io/playground/) now runs the same check as you type. Until
this week it did not. It called the parser and nothing else, so a typo'd key
showed as "Valid", and so did a route pointing at an upstream that doesn't
exist, which the proxy refuses to start with. Looking into that turned up one
more of our own: `service-type` was on the route's list of known keys, so lint
passed it, but the parser never read it, and `service-type "api"` (used
throughout our getting-started guide) left the route as `web`. Both are fixed
on main ([#514](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/pull/514)) and ship
in the next release.

### Validate every snippet in the docs

Configuration examples in documentation get copied into production, so they
are configuration. Since
[docs#71](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinelproxy.io-docs/pull/71), CI
downloads a pinned Zentinel release, runs `zentinel validate` and
`zentinel lint` against every `kdl` block in the documentation, and fails the
deploy on any error or any "is being ignored" warning. At merge it checked 569
snippets, 0 failing; partial examples are marked as fragments and skipped
explicitly rather than by accident.

The previous version of this check is a cautionary tale in its own right. It
"helpfully" rewrote common mistakes before validating, mapping `cert-path` to
`cert-file`, `workers` to `worker-threads`, and four others. Each rewrite turned
a snippet that was wrong on the page into one that validated. `cert-path` sat
green on two pages for months, describing an HTTPS listener with no
certificate. Those rewrites were removed in
[docs#54](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinelproxy.io-docs/pull/54). A
checker that corrects its input before checking it is checking its own
corrections.

## What is still open

This class is not closed, and it would undercut the point of this post to
pretend otherwise. As of 26.10_3, these are accepted without a lint warning
(tracked in [#521](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues/521)):

- `method "GET" "POST"` in a route's `matches` keeps only the first method.
- `load-balancing "least-connections"`, with a hyphen, falls back to round
  robin; only `least_connections` is recognised.
- A health check `type` that is not recognised becomes a TCP check.
- A run-together line inside `matches` is not reported, and the conditions
  after the first are dropped.

The docs checker already treats the first two as traps. A route's
`max-body-size` and `rate-limits { default-rps }` are parsed and never
enforced ([#517](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues/517),
[#518](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues/518)), and
`zentinel test` does not report ignored keys at all; only `lint` does
([#523](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues/523)). And `zentinel lint`
exits 0 on warnings, so a CI step that wants to fail on ignored keys has to
look for them, as the docs job does.

## Checking your own deployment

If you run Zentinel, two things are worth doing after reading this:

1. Run `zentinel lint -c <your config>` and read every line containing
   "is being ignored". Each one is a setting you wrote that is not in effect.
2. For the features you rely on most, check them at the far end rather than in
   the config: count health-check requests at a backend, stop an agent and see
   whether anything changes, send a request that should be retried to an
   upstream that fails on purpose.

If either turns up something that lint did not flag, we would like to hear about
it in an [issue](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues). That is how
most of the bugs above were found.

================================================================================

# Zentinel 26.09–26.10: Pingora 0.9, Health Checks That Probe, and a Security Sweep

URL: https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/zentinel-26-09-26-10/
Published: 2026-10-18

> Nine releases in seven weeks, from 26.09_1 to 26.10_3. Health checks that had never sent a probe now do, agents that restart are no longer lost, bundle install works for non-root users, the engine moves to Pingora 0.9.0, ACME renewal follows the CA's window, and 26.10_3 brings wasmtime 49 and rustls 0.23.46. Here is what changed and what to check when you upgrade.

Between 1 September and 18 October we shipped nine releases, 26.09_1 through
26.10_3 (crate versions 0.6.38 to 0.6.46). Some of them add things. More of them
fix things that looked like they worked and did not, and those are the ones this
post spends most of its time on, because they are the ones that change what your
deployment was actually doing.

If you only read one section, read the next one.

## Health checks never probed anything (26.09_2)

On 0.6.38 and earlier, every `health-check` block in every configuration was
inert. The active health checker built its backend set from the configured
targets but never populated the set that the probe loop iterates, so every cycle
checked zero backends — for `http`, `tcp`, `grpc` and `inference` checks alike.

It failed silently in both directions. No probe was sent, so a backend that was
down was never detected; and no backend was ever marked unhealthy, so nothing was
ever taken out of rotation. The runner started, logged that it had started, and
ticked on schedule, while the configuration and `zentinel lint` both reported
health checking as configured. Measured against a real backend at
`interval-secs 2`: 0 probes in twelve seconds before the fix, 29 after.

Anyone relying on health-checked failover did not have it. No configuration
change is needed: existing `health-check` blocks start working on upgrade.
**That also means backends that have been failing quietly may be marked unhealthy
and removed from rotation for the first time.** Check which backends are marked
unhealthy after upgrading rather than assuming nothing moved.

## Agents: sockets, restarts and installs

Three separate faults, each of which made agents appear to do nothing rather than
produce an error — and with `failure-mode "open"`, the default in the shipped
examples, traffic flowed unprocessed.

**Container images could not create agent sockets (26.09_3).** `/var/run/zentinel`
was not created in any image, so a Docker named volume mounted there came up
root-owned while the agent images run as `nonroot`. The bind failed, the proxy
had nothing to connect to, and every agent route failed open. The images now
create the directory, but because `/var/run` is a symlink to `/run` on both the
Debian and distroless bases, that is not a reliable fix on its own. If you write
your own Compose file, prepare the volume explicitly with an init container (the
shipped `docker-compose.yml` shows how, with mode `1777`).

**An agent the proxy could not reach at startup was lost until the proxy
restarted (26.09_4).** That covered an agent slower to start than the proxy, an
agent on a volume that was not ready yet, and any agent that *restarts* — a
crash, an upgrade, a rolling deploy. Four things had to change: unreachable
agents are now registered and marked unhealthy instead of refused, pool
maintenance starts independently of registration, reconnection no longer gives
up after three attempts (the attempt count now bounds the retry interval, capped
at two minutes), and a reconnected agent's capabilities are re-learned. If you
added start-ordering to work around this, it is no longer required.

**`zentinel bundle install` failed for every non-root user (26.09_5).** The
writability check asked "can anyone write here?" instead of "can I?", so
`/usr/local/bin` looked writable to everyone, the installer chose a system-wide
install, and then failed creating `/etc/zentinel/agents`. It now uses `access(2)`
on every directory the install creates. A user-local install goes to
`~/.local/bin` and `~/.config/zentinel/agents/`; use `--prefix` to choose
somewhere else. Reported by [@alanorth](https://github.com/alanorth), who also
noticed the registry pages named a path the installer has never used; all 23
agent pages were corrected.

## MCP gateway

The MCP work in 26.09_2 is covered in
[A Gateway for Agentic Protocols](https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/the-gateway-for-agentic-protocols/):
per-tool metrics (`zentinel_mcp_calls_total`, resolved from the body and bounded
by the route's configuration), per-tool rate limiting via the `mcp-tool` and
`client-ip-and-mcp-tool` keys, `tools/list` filtered to what the route permits,
and an MCP-native `health-check { type "mcp" }`.

Since then:

- **One route can front several MCP servers as a single endpoint (26.09_3).**
  `tools/list` merges every upstream's tools under a declared prefix, and a call
  is routed by that prefix. A `session-key` is required with two or more
  upstreams, and policy applies to the name the client sees
  (`deny "warehouse.execute_sql"`). An unreachable upstream costs its own tools
  in the listing and no others. Resources are refused on a multiplexing route,
  because a URI cannot carry an upstream prefix.
- **JSON-RPC response ids keep their type (26.09_3).** `"id": 42` had been
  answered as `"id": "42"`.
- **Multiplexed tool calls are proxied rather than originated (26.09_4)**, so
  they now use the connection pool, the route's retry policy and the upstream's
  TLS settings. Listings and the per-upstream `initialize` handshake are still
  composed by the proxy.

The configuration reference is in the
[agentic protocols docs](https://docs.zentinelproxy.io/configuration/agentic/).

## Pingora 0.9.0 (26.09_6)

The engine under Zentinel moved from Pingora 0.8.1 to
[0.9.0](https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora/releases/tag/0.9.0); our fork was
rebased in [zentinelproxy/pingora#10](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/pingora/pull/10)
and both fork patches carry over unchanged in behaviour. What it brings:

- Request-target hardening: path and authority validation share one parser,
  ambiguous authorities are rejected on ingress and egress, and CR/LF in an
  HTTP/2 `:path` is rejected.
- Hop-by-hop request headers are stripped before the upstream sees them, along
  with any header the client nominates in `Connection`. A request that nominates
  `Host`, a forwarding header or a pseudo-header-shaped name is rejected.
- HTTP/1 upstream connections are never reused after an incomplete response or a
  failed write.
- Default HTTP/2 server limits are bounded rather than unbounded.

One forwarding behaviour changes and is worth checking before you upgrade:
**WebSocket upgrades still work, but other HTTP/1 upgrades (for example `h2c`)
are no longer forwarded**, and `Proxy-Authorization` is not passed on. Nothing in
the configuration turns the old pass-through back on; if you depended on it,
[open an issue](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues). Cache keys
and on-disk hashes are unchanged, so no cache goes cold.

## ACME: renew when the CA suggests (26.10_2)

When the ACME server supports ACME Renewal Information
([RFC 9773](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9773)) — Let's Encrypt does —
Zentinel now asks the CA for its suggested renewal window and renews at a
uniformly random point inside it, so a fleet does not renew at the same moment.
`renew-before-days` stays a hard floor: ARI can make a renewal earlier, never
later. Renewal orders also name the certificate they replace, which at Let's
Encrypt exempts the renewal from rate limits. CAs without ARI behave as before.
No configuration change is needed. Thanks to
[@Curious-r](https://github.com/Curious-r) for this and the Cloudflare fix below.
See [the ACME docs](https://docs.zentinelproxy.io/configuration/listeners/#ca-suggested-renewal-windows-ari).

## Security and dependency sweep (26.09_1 to 26.10_3)

26.10_3 is mostly security updates in dependencies. Nothing in it changes how
Zentinel routes, inspects or blocks traffic.

- **`wasmtime` 48.0.0 → 49.0.3** for WASM agents: 23 advisories
  (RUSTSEC-2026-0314 to -0364), including a critical native stack buffer
  overflow (RUSTSEC-2026-0327) and a WASI filesystem sandbox escape
  (RUSTSEC-2026-0352). Only relevant if you run WASM agents.
- **`rustls` 0.23.46** (RUSTSEC-2026-0346 to -0349), mostly in rustls as a TLS
  client — the role Zentinel has toward upstreams, agents and the ACME server.
  26.10_1 had already taken 0.23.45, with stricter handling after a
  HelloRetryRequest.
- **`h2` 0.3.27 is gone** from the tree (RUSTSEC-2026-0258), and
  `crossbeam-epoch` moves to 0.9.21 (RUSTSEC-2026-0204). `cargo audit` is clean.
- **OpenTelemetry 0.33**, with no code changes needed.
- **`maxminddb` 0.32 (26.10_1)** bounds the work done decoding a crafted GeoIP
  database. The database is operator-supplied, so this matters only if its
  source is not fully trusted.

26.10_3 also fixes **Cloudflare DNS-01 for subdomains**: the provider looked up
only a zone named exactly like the certificate's domain, so `app.example.com`
could not be issued when the zone is `example.com`. It now walks up to the most
specific parent zone that exists, and still reports API and authentication
errors as errors.

**Building from source now needs Rust 1.96**, required by `wasmtime` 49.
Prebuilt binaries and container images are not affected.

## Upgrading

No release in this range needs a configuration change. Two things deserve a look
afterwards:

1. **Upstream health.** If you configure `health-check`, backends may be marked
   unhealthy for the first time.
2. **Non-WebSocket upgrades.** If any client relies on `Upgrade: h2c` or similar
   being forwarded, it no longer is.

The full detail, including everything we left out here, is in the
[CHANGELOG](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md),
and the general procedure is in the
[upgrade guide](https://docs.zentinelproxy.io/operations/upgrade-guide/).

---

*Zentinel 26.10_3 (crate 0.6.46) is on
[crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/zentinel-proxy) and
[GitHub](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/releases). Every release is
signed and ships with SBOMs; see [supply chain security](https://zentinelproxy.io/supply-chain/) for how
to verify it.*

================================================================================

# A Gateway for Agentic Protocols

URL: https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/the-gateway-for-agentic-protocols/
Published: 2026-09-02

> Zentinel now does for MCP what a reverse proxy has always done for HTTP: per-tool metrics, per-tool rate limits, a tool list cut to what the route permits, and a health check that speaks the protocol. Here is what shipped, two things it caught that had been silently broken for months, and an honest outlook on the harder question — whether a proxy should also be an MCP server.

Six months ago the interesting traffic through a reverse proxy was HTTP requests
from browsers. Increasingly it is JSON-RPC from models: an agent calling a tool,
an agent talking to another agent, a completion request billed by the token.
These are not HTTP-shaped problems wearing new names. A rate limit that counts
requests is close to meaningless when one request runs a database query and the
next returns a cached string.

We wrote about [the header/body desync in MCP](https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/header-says-read-body-says-delete/)
in August — the part where the protocol invites intermediaries to trust a header
that the client controls independently of the body. That post was about deciding
whether to forward a request. This one is about everything after that decision,
because guarding one MCP server is a fraction of what a gateway does.

Zentinel 26.09_2 adds four things. Each is a thing a reverse proxy has always
done for HTTP, done properly for MCP for the first time.

## Count what actually ran

`zentinel_mcp_calls_total` is labelled by route, JSON-RPC method, tool, and
decision:

```
zentinel_mcp_calls_total{route="mcp",method="tools/call",target="search_docs",decision="allowed"} 4213
zentinel_mcp_calls_total{route="mcp",method="tools/call",target="execute_sql",decision="denied"} 17
```

The method and tool come from the request **body**, never from the mirrored
`Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name` headers. This is the desync again, in its
observability costume: a client can set `Mcp-Name: search_docs` while the body
calls `execute_sql`, and a dashboard built on headers would show a tidy picture
of a tool that never ran.

Both labels are attacker-supplied, which makes cardinality a real concern rather
than a theoretical one — a client calling `tools/call` with random names could
otherwise mint an unbounded number of series and take the metrics endpoint with
it. So each label is reduced to something the route's own configuration names,
and anything else is reported as `<other>`. The number of series a route can
produce is bounded by its config, not by its traffic.

## Rate limit the expensive tool, not the endpoint

An MCP endpoint shares one limit across every tool it exposes. A client
hammering the tool that runs a query exhausts the quota for the tool that
returns a constant.

```kdl
filter "per-tool" {
    type "rate-limit"
    max-rps 5
    key "mcp-tool"
}
```

`mcp-tool` and `client-ip-and-mcp-tool` are the first rate-limit keys Zentinel
resolves from the request body rather than from headers, for the reason above: a
limit keyed on `Mcp-Name` would meter what a client claimed rather than what the
server will execute. The consequence is that the limit applies once the body has
arrived rather than on headers, which is a real difference and worth knowing —
it only applies to routes carrying an `mcp` block.

## Stop advertising what you will refuse

This one started as tidiness and turned out to be a disclosure.

A route with `tools { allow "search_docs" "get_weather" }` refuses a call to
anything else. Until now it also let the upstream answer `tools/list` with the
full set. A client would ask what is available, receive all eighty tools the
server offers, pick one of the seventy-five this route forbids, and be refused.
The policy held. Everything about the exchange was avoidable.

Three costs, in increasing order of how much they matter:

1. A wasted round trip whose failure reads as a bug in the upstream.
2. Tool descriptions spent from the model's context window. MCP clients degrade
   well before a hundred tools; a route permitting five of eighty should
   advertise five.
3. **A tool list is an inventory.** Names and descriptions routinely say which
   internal systems exist and what they can be made to do. A client permitted to
   call none of them still got to read all of it.

`tools/list`, `resources/list` and `prompts/list` responses are now filtered to
exactly what the route permits — same identity rule, same predicate as the
enforcer, so what is hidden is precisely what a call would be refused and never
more. A filter that hid a *different* set than the enforcer refuses would be
worse than no filter: it would make the advertised surface actively misleading
rather than merely incomplete.

## Health checks that speak the protocol

A TCP check proves a socket is open. An HTTP check proves something answered
200. Neither says the thing behind it still speaks MCP — and plenty of MCP
servers expose no `/health` endpoint at all, so for an upstream whose entire
purpose is serving tool calls, the usual checks confirm the least interesting
property available.

```kdl
health-check {
    type "mcp" {
        path "/mcp"
        expected-tools "search_docs" "get_weather"
    }
    interval-secs 30
}
```

The probe sends `initialize`, and given `expected-tools` also asks `tools/list`
and requires those tools to be present. A server that is listening and
initialising but has lost the backend behind its tools is marked unhealthy and
taken out of rotation, rather than left there to fail real calls. A JSON-RPC
error counts as unhealthy despite arriving with HTTP 200 — which is the failure
mode a plain HTTP check structurally cannot see.

## What we found while building it

Two things worth reporting, because both had been true for a long time and
neither produced an error.

**Health checks never probed anything.** Not the MCP ones — *any* of them.
`http`, `tcp`, `grpc`, `inference`, in every configuration. The runner spawned,
logged that it had started, and ticked on schedule against an empty backend set.
Measured against a real backend at `interval-secs 2`: zero probes in twelve
seconds.

It failed silently in both directions, which is why it lasted. No probe was
sent, so a backend that was down was never detected. No backend was ever marked
unhealthy, so nothing was taken out of rotation. Anyone who configured
health-checked failover had the appearance of it and not the fact. The fix is in
this release, and it is worth knowing what to expect on upgrade: backends that
have been quietly failing may be marked unhealthy and removed from rotation for
the first time.

**Our own integration suite had never run.** It existed, it was thorough, and CI
executed `cargo test` only. Wiring it up surfaced four further faults *in the
suite itself* — it terminated on its first passing assertion, probed the wrong
port, lacked routes for the paths it asserted on, and could not reach the agent
it was testing. Every property it covers had been unverified between releases.

There is a pattern here we keep meeting: code that parses, starts, logs, and
does nothing. It does not show up in tests that check configuration, because the
configuration is correct. It shows up when you count the requests arriving at the
other end.

## MCP is not the only protocol

The same machinery is not MCP-specific by accident.

**A2A** gets method allow/deny lists and explicit handling of methods the proxy
does not recognise — defaulting to allow, deliberately, because A2A is young and
refusing every method added after the proxy was built would make upgrading your
agents require upgrading your proxy first.

**Inference upstreams** get token-aware load balancing (`least_tokens_queued`,
which balances on queued work rather than connection count), token budgets, and
health checks that verify the models you depend on are actually loaded rather
than that the server is up.

## Where this goes: Zentinel as an MCP origin

Everything above is Zentinel as a **gateway**. It sits in front of an MCP server
and enforces, meters and observes. It is not an MCP server itself, and today it
cannot be one.

The question we keep being asked — and keep asking ourselves — is whether it
should be. Here is our current thinking, offered as an outlook rather than a
roadmap, because none of it is built and some of it may not survive contact with
the design.

### The gap

Most MCP-worthy context is not an HTTP API. It is object storage, a filesystem,
a SQL database, a search index, a pile of internal documentation. MCP is how a
model reaches all of it, and today reaching any of it means writing a server.

That work gets rewritten per organisation, and the artifact it produces is
usually a process holding broad credentials with no policy in front of it —
precisely the thing a proxy exists to sit in front of. The pitch is not
"REST → MCP"; several tools do that already. It is that a server declared in
Zentinel's config would be **policy-enforced from its first request**, because
the engine described in the rest of this post is already here. The allowlists,
the per-tool metrics, the rate limits, the audit trail — none of that would need
building again.

### The shape it would take

Tools and resources come from a **closed, curated set of sources**, declared in
configuration:

| Source | Exposes as |
|---|---|
| `http` / OpenAPI | tools, from operations you name |
| `filesystem` / object store | resources |
| `sql` | tools, from named parameterised read-only queries |
| `search` index | tools |
| an existing Zentinel `agent` | tools |

Sketching it — **this is illustrative, not a spec, and no part of it works
today**:

```kdl
mcp-server "internal" {
    source "docs" {
        type "search"
        tool "search_runbooks" {
            description "Search operational runbooks by keyword"
        }
    }
    source "reporting" {
        type "sql"
        read-only #true
        tool "revenue_by_month" {
            description "Monthly revenue for a given year"
            query "SELECT month, total FROM revenue WHERE year = $1"
        }
    }
}
```

Two properties of that sketch matter more than the syntax.

**Every tool is named by a human.** There is no mode where pointing at an
OpenAPI spec generates two hundred tools. Whole-spec generation is at most a
scaffolding command that emits config for you to review, edit and commit —
never a live binding. A tool surface that changes because someone edited a spec
in another repository is implicit behaviour of the worst kind, and it is the
single thing we are most determined not to ship.

**The source list is closed.** "A place to embed arbitrary logic because it
might be useful" is how a bounded system stops being one. No scripting in
config, no shell-command source. If your case needs one, an
[agent](https://docs.zentinelproxy.io/agents/) is the extension point and always
has been.

### What we would get wrong if we hurried

Four problems we would rather solve on paper first.

**Tool-count explosion.** A real API becomes hundreds of tools, and MCP clients
degrade badly past a few dozen because the tool list eats the model's context
window. This is the strongest argument that *curation is the product* — the
valuable artifact is a short, well-described tool list, not a complete one. It
also means the tool-list filtering shipped in this release is not a side feature
of the gateway; it is the same insight arriving early.

**Names and descriptions dominate quality.** Model tool-selection depends on them
far more than on schema correctness, and names auto-derived from `operationId`
are reliably poor. This cuts the same way: a generator that produces
`getUserByIdV2` for two hundred endpoints has produced something worse than
nothing.

**Side effects.** Every `DELETE` endpoint becomes callable the moment it becomes
a tool. Allowlist-by-default is not a setting here, it is the only defensible
default — along with read-only by default for `sql` and `filesystem`.

**Session state.** MCP has sessions; a reverse proxy is comfortably stateless.
This is the one genuinely blocking question, and it blocks the *gateway* half
too — presenting several MCP servers as one endpoint with their tools namespaced
apart needs an answer to where a session lives and what happens when one
upstream dies mid-session. Whatever we decide shapes everything built on top, so
we would rather settle it before writing code than during.

### Where it would live

Not in the proxy hot path. Serving MCP inverts what the proxy is — it stops
forwarding and starts originating — so this belongs in an agent or a distinct
`serve` mode. Agents can already short-circuit with a response, which makes it
feasible without touching request forwarding, and keeping it out of the hot path
keeps the gateway work shippable on its own. Which is exactly what happened this
release.

### Honestly

Zentinel is a proxy. The gateway work in this post is unambiguously proxy work:
it is what a reverse proxy does, applied to a protocol that did not exist when
most reverse proxies were written. Originating MCP is a different claim, and
"our proxy is also an application server" is a sentence that has ended badly for
other projects.

We think there is a real version of it — narrow, declarative, curated, and
policy-enforced from the first request — and we would rather build that one
slowly than a general one quickly. The scope discipline we have written down for
ourselves is to prove it with exactly two sources, `http` and one non-API, before
adding a third.

It is all tracked in
[#443](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel/issues/443). If you are running
MCP behind a proxy, or want to, that issue is the right place to tell us which
half matters more to you — and which two sources you would actually use. That
answer would change what we build first.

---

*Zentinel 26.09_2 is on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/zentinel-proxy) and
[GitHub](https://github.com/zentinelproxy/zentinel). The MCP configuration
reference is in [the docs](https://docs.zentinelproxy.io/configuration/agentic/).*

================================================================================

# Header Says Read, Body Says Delete

URL: https://zentinelproxy.io/blog/header-says-read-body-says-delete/
Published: 2026-08-23
Updated: 2026-08-25

> MCP's Streamable HTTP transport mirrors the tool name into an HTTP header so that gateways can route without parsing the body. Read that header and enforce policy on it, and you have built an allowlist that allows everything. Here's the desync, the version-downgrade that defeats the obvious fix, and what Zentinel does instead.

> **Correction — 25 August 2026.** When this was published, the enforcement described below **did not run**. The configuration parsed and the policy engine was correct; nothing in the request path ever called it. It was fixed in Zentinel 0.6.28, released the next day. The original text is left intact; the full account is [at the end](#the-correction).

A protocol that tells intermediaries "you can trust this header instead of reading the body" is doing something genuinely useful and quietly dangerous. Useful, because parsing a JSON body on every request to make a routing decision is real cost a gateway would rather not pay. Dangerous, because the moment there are two sources of truth for what a request does, an attacker gets to pick which one you read.

The Model Context Protocol does exactly this, deliberately and for good reasons. We implemented MCP awareness in Zentinel last week, and the interesting part of the work was not parsing JSON-RPC. It was working out which of the things MCP hands you are safe to believe.

## The shortcut

MCP's Streamable HTTP transport mirrors selected fields from the request body into HTTP headers. From the specification:

> The Streamable HTTP transport mirrors selected JSON-RPC body fields into HTTP headers so that intermediaries (load balancers, gateways, observability tooling) can route and inspect requests without parsing the body.

Concretely, a tool call arrives looking like this:

```http
POST /mcp HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28
Mcp-Method: tools/call
Mcp-Name: get_weather

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": { "name": "get_weather", "arguments": { "location": "Seattle, WA" } }
}
```

`Mcp-Method` mirrors `method`. `Mcp-Name` mirrors `params.name`. If you are a proxy that wants to allowlist which tools a client may call, this is exactly the information you need, sitting in a header, already parsed by your HTTP stack.

The temptation is obvious. So is the bug.

## The desync

```http
POST /mcp HTTP/1.1
MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28
Mcp-Method: tools/call
Mcp-Name: read_file

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call",
 "params":{"name":"delete_everything"}}
```

The gateway reads `Mcp-Name: read_file`, checks it against the allowlist, forwards. The server reads `params.name`, and deletes everything.

There is no exploit code here. There is no parser bug, no encoding trick, no race. There are two fields that are supposed to be equal, and a request in which they are not.

The specification is aware of this. It requires *servers* to reject mismatches with a dedicated error code, `-32020 HeaderMismatch`, and explains why in terms that name the exact scenario:

> This prevents potential security vulnerabilities when different components in the network rely on different sources of truth (e.g., a load balancer routing on the header value while the MCP server executes based on the body value).

So a conforming server catches this. The problem is that "conforming server" is doing load-bearing work in that sentence. Your gateway's allowlist is a security control precisely because you do not want to rely on the thing behind it behaving correctly — that is what a gateway is *for*. A control that only works when the protected system is also correct is not much of a control.

## The obvious fix, and why it isn't enough

Compare the header to the body. If they disagree, refuse the request.

That is right, and it is what Zentinel does. But implemented on its own it is defeated by one header:

```http
MCP-Protocol-Version: 2025-06-18
Mcp-Method: tools/call
Mcp-Name: read_file

{"params":{"name":"delete_everything"}}
```

Protocol revisions before `2026-07-28` did not require mirrored headers to match the body. Some did not define these headers at all. So a proxy that validates header against body has to decide what to do when the request claims a revision where that requirement never existed — and if the answer is "skip the check", the check is optional at the attacker's discretion.

The specification anticipates this too, in a note aimed squarely at people building what we were building:

> Intermediaries that enforce policy based on mirrored headers (e.g., routing or rate-limiting by tenant) **SHOULD** verify that the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header indicates a version that requires header–body validation. If the version is older or the header is absent, the intermediary **SHOULD** reject the request rather than trusting unvalidated header values.

This is the part we expect implementers to miss. The first half — compare header to body — is the intuitive move, and it *feels* complete. The second half is a statement about the space of protocol versions, which is not where anyone's attention is when they are writing a policy engine.

Zentinel refuses requests claiming a revision older than `2026-07-28` by default. You can turn that off with `require-validated-version #false`, and the documentation says plainly what you are accepting when you do.

## The third header nobody talks about

While reviewing our own implementation before opening the pull request, we found we had done the same thing we were writing a module to prevent.

MCP lets a tool schema mark individual **arguments** for mirroring, via an `x-mcp-header` annotation. The specification's own worked example is a SQL tool that mirrors its region:

```http
Mcp-Method: tools/call
Mcp-Name: execute_sql
Mcp-Param-Region: us-west1

{"params":{"name":"execute_sql",
 "arguments":{"region":"us-west1","query":"SELECT * FROM users"}}}
```

Routing by region is precisely the use case the spec offers for these headers. Which means `Mcp-Param-Region: us-west1` with a body saying `eu-central-1` sends the request to one place and executes it in another — the same defect, on a header that is easier to overlook because it is defined by a tool's schema rather than by the protocol.

We had validated `Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name` and stopped there. Two of three.

Fixing it surfaced a genuine limitation worth stating rather than papering over. The header's *name* comes from the `x-mcp-header` label in the tool's schema, and that label is not required to equal the property name — `x-mcp-header: "Region"` on a property called `region` is the spec's example, but `x-mcp-header: "Reg"` would be equally valid. A proxy has never seen that schema. So Zentinel checks the headers whose suffix matches an argument name and leaves the rest alone, because denying an unmatched header would refuse legitimate traffic over a naming convention it cannot see.

That is a hole, and we would rather document it than pretend otherwise: **if you route or rate-limit on `Mcp-Param-*` headers, keep the label equal to the property name**, or the proxy cannot confirm the two still agree.

## What we actually built

The rule that falls out of all of this is short:

**Policy resolves against the body. Headers are consulted only to confirm they agree with it.**

Not "prefer the body". Not "check the header, fall back to the body". The body decides, always, and a header that disagrees is not a formatting problem to be normalised away — it is a request that contradicts itself, and it gets refused:

```
mcp-name header says "read_file" but the request body says "delete_everything";
policy is resolved against the body, and a request that disagrees with itself
is refused
```

We treat mismatches as hostile rather than as client bugs. From inside the proxy the two are indistinguishable — a buggy client and an attacker produce byte-identical requests — and only one of them is dangerous. Denying both costs a broken client an error message. Allowing both costs you the allowlist.

The performance argument for reading the header instead of the body turns out to be weaker than it looks, incidentally. You are already terminating TLS, already parsing HTTP, already buffering the body to forward it. Reading `params.name` out of a JSON object you have in memory is not the expensive part of anything.

## A2A, briefly

We added Agent2Agent support in the same change, and it is *simpler to police* for one reason: it has no mirrored headers. The method is in the body, and only in the body.

There is nothing to desynchronise, so there is nothing to spoof. The lesson generalises past MCP: giving an intermediary a second, cheaper source of truth is a feature that creates an attack surface, and a protocol that declines to offer one is easier to put a gateway in front of.

## The pattern underneath

This was not an isolated find. It came at the end of a week in which we found **thirteen** instances of the same shape in Zentinel's own configuration handling — settings that parsed cleanly, validated cleanly, and did nothing:

- Every upstream timeout in every shipped config was being discarded and replaced by its default. The parser read `connect`, the configs wrote `connect-secs`. An inference example asking for `request-secs 300` was cutting requests off at sixty.
- `failure-mode "open"` was pinned to `closed` regardless of configuration, because the parser never populated the field. Routes deliberately set to fail open would block traffic when an agent died.
- A `require_auth` flag that checked a token was *present* and never that it was *correct*. Any non-empty string authenticated.
- `client-auth` without a `ca-file` logged a warning and served ordinary TLS, so an operator could configure mutual TLS, pass `zentinel validate`, start the proxy, and accept unauthenticated clients.

Different subsystems, different authors, one shape: **the configuration says a thing is happening, and it is not.**

## The one lesson worth taking

Three of those thirteen hid the same way, and they are the reason we now have a rule.

`idle-timeout-secs 60` looked correct because the parser's default was also 60. `redis-fallback-local #true` looked correct because the default was true. `memcached-ttl-secs 2` looked correct because the default was 2. In each case the setting was being thrown away, and in each case the discarded value happened to equal what the code would have done anyway — so parsing the shipped config and eyeballing the result confirmed nothing at all.

We know exactly how well that trap works, because it caught us mid-investigation. We published a correction saying `memcached-ttl-secs` was fine, then had to retract it two hours later after testing it properly.

**Verify against a value that differs from the default.** Checking `timeout-secs 30` against a default of 30 proves nothing. Checking it against 7 proves everything.

The same rule applies to test suites, which is where it bit hardest. An existing test called `accepts_valid_auth_token` had been passing for months against an implementation that authenticated nothing:

```rust
let config = ReverseConnectionConfig {
    require_auth: true,
    ..Default::default()          // no tokens configured. none. anywhere.
};
request.auth_token = Some("valid-token-123".to_string());   // never configured
assert!(result.is_ok());
```

It configured no tokens, sent a string that existed nowhere, and asserted acceptance — and passed, because presence was the only check.
